# Exercise 2.4 — Imputation {#sec-imputation}

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- quantify how much data you would lose by dropping every incomplete row;
- fill missing values with a mean or a median, and measure what that does to
  the spread of the column;
- say why the median is the safer default for a skewed variable;
- explain what iterative imputation does differently, and what it assumes;
- argue for leaving a value missing rather than inventing one.

## Why this, here

@sec-cleaning left the extract clean but incomplete. The missing-value codes
are now real missing values, which means they can finally be counted — and
something has to be decided about them, because most models will not accept a
missing value at all.

This exercise is deliberately partial. It works two approaches through
properly, in one language each, and leaves the rest for you to try. Mean and
median imputation are shown in R; iterative imputation is shown in Python. The
tasks ask you to produce the missing halves. That is the point: by now you have
seen enough of both languages that translating a method you understand is a
reasonable thing to ask.

## Starting point

Each chapter stands alone, so we reload and repeat the cleaning from
@sec-cleaning in one block.

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Python**

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

num_cols = ["age", "bmi", "bp_systolic"]
ref_map = {
    "GP": "GP", "gp": "GP",
    "General Practitioner": "GP",
    "A&E": "A&E",
    "Self-referral": "Self-referral",
}

clinic = pd.read_csv(
    "data/clinic_extract.csv"
)
for c in num_cols:
    clinic[c] = pd.to_numeric(
        clinic[c], errors="coerce"
    )
clinic["referral_source"] = (
    clinic["referral_source"].map(ref_map)
)
clinic.shape
```
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**R**

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

num_cols <- c("age", "bmi", "bp_systolic")

clinic <- read_csv(
  "data/clinic_extract.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(across(
    all_of(num_cols),
    ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))
  )) |>
  mutate(referral_source = recode(
    referral_source,
    "gp" = "GP",
    "General Practitioner" = "GP"
  ))
dim(clinic)
```
:::
::::::

### How much is missing, and where

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Python**

```{python}
print(clinic[num_cols].isna().sum())
print("complete rows:",
      clinic.dropna().shape[0],
      "of", clinic.shape[0])
```
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**R**

```{r}
print(colSums(is.na(clinic[num_cols])))
cat("complete rows:",
    sum(complete.cases(clinic)),
    "of", nrow(clinic), "\n")
```
:::
::::::

Note the arithmetic. The three columns are missing different numbers of values,
but the count of complete rows is lower than any of them individually, because
the gaps fall in different rows. This is the first argument against dropping
incomplete rows: the loss compounds across columns, and it compounds faster the
more columns you have.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Mean and median imputation, in R

The idea is the simplest one available: put the column's own average where a
value is missing. It needs no model, no package, and one line.

```{r}
imp_mean <- clinic |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols),
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

imp_median <- clinic |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols),
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

cat("missing left, mean:  ", sum(is.na(imp_mean[num_cols])), "\n")
cat("missing left, median:", sum(is.na(imp_median[num_cols])), "\n")
```

### What it did to the spread

Filling 9 values of `bmi` with one single number means nine rows now sit
exactly on top of each other. The column's standard deviation must fall.
Measure it rather than taking it on trust:

```{r}
comparison <- data.frame(
  column    = num_cols,
  sd_before = sapply(clinic[num_cols], sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd_mean   = sapply(imp_mean[num_cols], sd),
  sd_median = sapply(imp_median[num_cols], sd)
)
comparison$pct_change_mean <- round(
  100 * (comparison$sd_mean - comparison$sd_before) / comparison$sd_before, 1)
comparison
```

Every standard deviation shrank. That matters because a standard deviation is
what a confidence interval is built from: impute the mean into 10% of a column
and every interval computed from it afterwards is narrower than the evidence
justifies. You have not added information, but you have made the data look as
though you had.

### Why median, for this column

`bmi` is right-skewed and contains one implausible value of 61.2. The mean is
pulled upward by it; the median is not.

```{r}
cat("bmi mean  :", round(mean(clinic$bmi, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("bmi median:", round(median(clinic$bmi, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
```

Every imputed `bmi` inherits whichever of those you chose. With a skewed
column, the mean puts nine patients at a value that more than half the cohort
sits below.

See it as a distribution. Nine values at one number do not announce themselves
in a histogram of the finished column — they land inside the existing peak and
disappear. So colour them:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
imp_mean |>
  mutate(source = if_else(is.na(clinic$bmi), "imputed", "observed")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(imputed = "#c0392b", observed = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "bmi", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

That is the honest picture, and it is also the warning: had you not kept track
of which rows you filled, nothing in the finished column would tell you. A
column of imputed values looks exactly like a column of measurements. Record
which is which — a `bmi_was_missing` indicator costs one column and keeps the
distinction available to everything downstream.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Iterative imputation, in Python

Mean imputation ignores every other column. If a patient's `bmi` is missing but
their `age` and `bp_systolic` are recorded, those two carry information about
the likely `bmi`, and the mean throws it away.

Iterative imputation uses it. It models each column with missing values as a
function of the other columns, predicts the gaps, and repeats — each round
using the previous round's filled-in values — until the estimates settle. In
scikit-learn it is still marked experimental, so it has to be enabled
explicitly.

```{python}
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer

imp = IterativeImputer(random_state=42, max_iter=20)
filled = imp.fit_transform(clinic[num_cols])

imp_iter = clinic.copy()
imp_iter[num_cols] = filled
print("missing left:", int(imp_iter[num_cols].isna().sum().sum()))
print("iterations run:", imp.n_iter_)
```

`max_iter` was 20 and it stopped well before that: with three columns and few
gaps there is very little for the rounds to refine, so the estimates stop
moving almost immediately. Read the number as a diagnostic — on a wide table it
would be larger, and an imputer that runs to `max_iter` without settling is
telling you something.

Compare what the two approaches put in the same cells:

```{python}
gaps = clinic["bmi"].isna()
side_by_side = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": clinic.loc[gaps, "age"],
    "bp": clinic.loc[gaps, "bp_systolic"],
    "mean_filled": clinic["bmi"].mean(),
    "iter_filled": imp_iter.loc[gaps, "bmi"].round(1),
})
side_by_side.head(9)
```

The mean column is one number repeated. The iterative column varies, because
it is reading each patient's other measurements. Whether it varies *correctly*
is a different question — it is a model, and it carries a model's assumptions:
that the columns are related in a way the imputer can represent, and that the
missingness does not itself depend on the value that is missing.

For this dataset we happen to know the second assumption holds, because
`data/PROVENANCE.txt` records that values were blanked out at random after the
outcome was generated. On real data you would not know that, and you would have
to argue for it.

## Task 1 — The approach neither section used

Dropping every incomplete row is the default in a surprising amount of
published analysis, usually silently. Quantify it.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
kept = clinic.______()
print(kept.shape[0], "of", clinic.shape[0])
print("lost:", round(100 * (1 - kept.shape[0] / clinic.shape[0]), 1), "%")

# Did dropping change who is in the data?
print(clinic["outcome"].mean().round(3))
print(kept["______"].mean().round(3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the method that removes rows containing any missing value.
The last is the outcome column, so you can compare its rate before and after.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
kept = clinic.dropna()
print(kept.shape[0], "of", clinic.shape[0])
print("lost:", round(100 * (1 - kept.shape[0] / clinic.shape[0]), 1), "%")

print(clinic["outcome"].mean().round(3))
print(kept["outcome"].mean().round(3))
```

Around a fifth of the cohort goes. The outcome rate barely moves here, which is
what you expect when values were blanked out at random — and is exactly what
you cannot count on when they were not.
:::
:::

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
kept <- clinic |> filter(______(clinic))
cat(nrow(kept), "of", nrow(clinic), "\n")
cat("lost:", round(100 * (1 - nrow(kept) / nrow(clinic)), 1), "%\n")

# Most-frequent-category imputation, for a categorical column
mode_site <- names(sort(table(clinic$hospital_site), decreasing = ______))[1]
mode_site
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the function returning TRUE for rows with no missing value
anywhere. For the second, you want the *largest* count first.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
kept <- clinic |> filter(complete.cases(clinic))
cat(nrow(kept), "of", nrow(clinic), "\n")
cat("lost:", round(100 * (1 - nrow(kept) / nrow(clinic)), 1), "%\n")

mode_site <- names(sort(table(clinic$hospital_site), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
mode_site
```

Most-frequent-category imputation is the categorical analogue of the mean, and
it has the same defect in a sharper form: it makes the commonest category
commoner, which is precisely the direction that hides a minority group.
:::
:::
:::

## Task 2 — Translate the other half

Each language above did only one thing. Produce the other.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python

Write mean and median imputation in Python and reproduce the standard-deviation
comparison from the R section.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
imp_mean_py = clinic.copy()
imp_mean_py[num_cols] = clinic[num_cols].fillna(
    clinic[num_cols].______()
)

sd_before = clinic[num_cols].std()
sd_after = imp_mean_py[num_cols].______()
print((100 * (sd_after - sd_before) / sd_before).round(1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks are the same kind of thing: the first is the statistic you are
filling with, the second is the one you are measuring. `fillna` accepts a
Series of per-column values.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
imp_mean_py = clinic.copy()
imp_mean_py[num_cols] = clinic[num_cols].fillna(clinic[num_cols].mean())

sd_before = clinic[num_cols].std()
sd_after = imp_mean_py[num_cols].std()
print((100 * (sd_after - sd_before) / sd_before).round(1))
```

The same shrinkage, to the same degree, by a different route.
:::
:::

## R

Iterative imputation in R lives in the `mice` package, whose default method for
a numeric column is predictive mean matching rather than a regression
prediction. Run it if `mice` is installed; read the answer if not.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(mice)
fit <- mice(clinic[______], m = 1, maxit = 10, printFlag = FALSE)
imp_iter_r <- complete(fit)
sum(is.na(imp_iter_r))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Pass the same three numeric columns the Python side used. `mice` will not
impute a patient identifier and should not be shown one.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(mice)
fit <- mice(clinic[num_cols], m = 1, maxit = 10, printFlag = FALSE)
imp_iter_r <- complete(fit)
sum(is.na(imp_iter_r))
```

One difference worth noticing: `mice` is built to produce *several* completed
datasets, not one. `m = 1` above asks it to behave like scikit-learn's imputer,
which is convenient here and throws away the thing `mice` exists to give you —
a measure of how uncertain each filled-in value was.
:::
:::
:::

## Reflection

1. Three columns were missing 11, 9 and 13 values, yet more than 11, 9 or 13
   rows were incomplete. Explain the arithmetic to someone who has not seen the
   data, and say what it implies for a dataset with 50 columns.
2. Mean imputation shrank every standard deviation. Name one statistic you
   would report after imputing that would now be wrong, and say in which
   direction.
3. The iterative imputer produced a different value for each patient. Give one
   reason that is better than a single repeated number, and one reason it could
   be worse.
4. Under what circumstance is leaving a value missing — and telling the reader
   it is missing — a better answer than any of the methods here?

## Stretch

### Stretch 1 — Make the imputation wrong on purpose
The values in this file were blanked out at random. Blank out `bmi` instead
for the patients with the highest `bp_systolic`, then impute with the mean and
compare the imputed values against the ones you deleted. You know the truth,
so you can measure the error — and see how an assumption of random missingness
fails when it is not true.

### Stretch 2 — Does better imputation buy a better model?
Fit the same classifier on the mean-imputed and the iteratively imputed data
and compare the test-set accuracy. Form a view before you run it. Then consider
how much of any difference you would be willing to attribute to the imputer,
given that the comparison rests on one split.

## What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the extract is now complete: no model will refuse it, and you can
state exactly which values were observed and which you supplied, and by what
rule.

You cannot say the imputed values are correct. They are estimates, and the mean
and median versions are estimates that ignore every other column in the table.
You also cannot claim your downstream uncertainty is honest — the shrinkage you
measured is still there.

And once again, none of this was done safely. Every mean, median and iterative
model above was fitted to all 150 rows. That is @sec-pipeline-steps.
